lessons.title: Lymphatic vessels and ducts
lessons.summary: Lymph returns to venous blood through collecting vessels and ducts.
recognitionCues: Capillaries are blind-ended.
landmarks: Thoracic duct drains most of the body.
relationships: Lymph flow is one-way toward venous angles.
commonConfusions: A duct is larger than a capillary.

lessons.title: Lymph node architecture
lessons.summary: Nodes filter lymph through organized cortical and medullary compartments.
recognitionCues: Afferent vessels enter; efferent vessels leave at the hilum; named node groups follow drainage regions.
Cervical, axillary, and inguinal nodes are named for head/neck, upper-limb, and lower-limb drainage regions.
landmarks: Subcapsular sinus lies beneath the capsule; cortical and medullary sinuses continue toward the hilum.
The capsule encloses cortex; medulla lies deeper and contains cords and sinuses near the hilum.
relationships: Cortex contains follicles, while medullary cords and sinuses lead to efferent drainage.
commonConfusions: Afferent and efferent directions are opposite; a sinus is not a vessel; a node group is not a single sinus.

lessons.title: Spleen architecture
lessons.summary: White pulp supports immune surveillance while red pulp filters blood.
recognitionCues: White pulp surrounds a central arteriole; red pulp contains cords and sinusoids.
The central arteriole is embedded in white pulp; the marginal zone forms its border with red pulp.
landmarks: The marginal zone lies between white and red pulp; splenic cords lie between sinusoids.
Red pulp is organized into splenic cords and vascular sinusoids rather than lymph-node sinuses.
relationships: Spleen filters blood rather than lymph, with arterial blood passing from white pulp toward red pulp.
commonConfusions: White pulp is not a lymph-node cortex; a central arteriole is not a node vessel; splenic sinusoids are not lymphatic sinuses.

lessons.title: Thymus architecture
lessons.summary: Thymic lobules contain a dark cortex and lighter medulla with Hassall corpuscles.
recognitionCues: Hassall corpuscles are medullary.
landmarks: Cortex is peripheral to medulla in a lobule.
relationships: Thymus is a primary lymphoid organ.
commonConfusions: Thymic cortex is not splenic red pulp.

lessons.title: Tonsils and MALT
lessons.summary: Tonsils and mucosal lymphoid aggregates monitor exposed epithelial surfaces.
recognitionCues: Tonsils ring the pharyngeal entrance.
landmarks: Pharyngeal tonsil is also called adenoid.
relationships: MALT is positioned at mucosal surfaces.
commonConfusions: A tonsil is not a lymphatic duct.

lessons.title: Intestinal lymphatics
lessons.summary: Lacteals and Peyer patches combine lipid uptake with mucosal immune surveillance.
recognitionCues: Lacteals lie in intestinal villi.
landmarks: Peyer patches are prominent in ileal mucosa; intestinal lymphatics converge toward the intestinal trunk.
relationships: Lacteals absorb dietary lipids; MALT samples antigens.
commonConfusions: A lacteal is not a blood capillary.

lessons.title: Lymphatic trunks and regional drainage
lessons.summary: Named trunks collect lymph from body regions before entering the major ducts.
recognitionCues: Jugular and subclavian trunks drain head/neck and upper limb regions; lumbar trunks converge on the cisterna chyli.
The intestinal trunk collects abdominal lymph, including lipid-rich lymph from intestinal lacteals.
landmarks: The cisterna chyli is the inferior origin of the thoracic duct; lumbar trunks enter it from the lower body.
relationships: Trunks converge into ducts that return lymph at the venous angles; jugular and subclavian trunks usually join near the root of the neck.
commonConfusions: A trunk is not a node; the right lymphatic duct is regional, not the main body duct; cisterna chyli is not a trunk.

lessons.title: Central endocrine control
lessons.summary: Hypothalamic neurons regulate pituitary tissue through distinct vascular and neural routes.
recognitionCues: Anterior and posterior pituitary are different tissues; pars intermedia is the narrow intervening zone.
landmarks: The stalk connects hypothalamus and pituitary.
relationships: Portal blood reaches anterior pituitary; axons reach posterior pituitary.
commonConfusions: Posterior pituitary is not a separate gland; pars intermedia is not the medulla.

lessons.title: Thyroid and parathyroid histology
lessons.summary: Follicles and chief cells distinguish the two adjacent neck endocrine organs.
recognitionCues: Colloid is inside a follicle; chief cells are in parathyroid tissue.
A thyroid lobe is a lateral mass; the isthmus is the midline bridge.
landmarks: Two thyroid lobes are joined anteriorly by the isthmus; parathyroids lie posteriorly.
A follicle is a spherical unit lined by follicular cells and filled with colloid.
relationships: Follicular cells surround colloid; parafollicular cells lie between follicles; parathyroid chief cells form the characteristic parathyroid population.
commonConfusions: Colloid is not a cell; the isthmus is not a lobe; parathyroid tissue is not a thyroid follicle.

lessons.title: Adrenal cortex and medulla
lessons.summary: The adrenal cortex has three zones external to a medulla containing chromaffin cells.
recognitionCues: Cortex is zonal; medulla is central.
The cortex forms the outer shell of the gland; chromaffin cells identify the inner medulla.

Gray1121 supports only gross adrenal location: suprarenal glands lie superior and medial to the kidneys beside the great vessels; it does not depict cortex, medulla, cortical zones, or chromaffin histology.
landmarks: Glomerulosa is outermost and reticularis deepest cortical zone.
The zones run from capsule inward: glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis, then medulla.
relationships: Cortex surrounds medulla; each cortical zone is a subdivision of the cortex, not a separate gland.
Use Gray1121 only for the gross suprarenal relationship to kidneys and great vessels, not for adrenal cortex, medulla, zones, or chromaffin cells.
commonConfusions: Zona fasciculata is not the medulla; chromaffin cells are not cortical cells.

lessons.title: Pancreatic and gonadal endocrine tissue
lessons.summary: Islets and gonadal interstitial tissues are endocrine components of organs with other functions.
recognitionCues: Islets are pale clusters among pancreatic acini.
landmarks: Corpus luteum follows ovulation; Leydig cells occupy testicular interstitium.
relationships: Beta, alpha, and delta cells occupy one islet but have different products.
commonConfusions: Sertoli cells are not Leydig cells.

lessons.title: Pineal and thymus
lessons.summary: Pineal and thymic tissues are recognizable endocrine-related organs outside the neck.
recognitionCues: The thymus is lobulated; the pineal is a small brain structure.
landmarks: Thymus lies in the anterior mediastinum.
relationships: Both are endocrine-related but have distinct locations and roles.
commonConfusions: Thymus is not a thyroid lobe.

lessons.title: Endocrine versus exocrine glands
lessons.summary: Duct presence separates endocrine secretion into blood from exocrine secretion through ducts.
recognitionCues: Endocrine tissue is ductless.
landmarks: The pancreas contains both components.
relationships: The same organ can have endocrine and exocrine regions.
commonConfusions: Ductless does not mean secretion is absent.

lessons.title: Heart orientation
lessons.summary: The apex, base, surfaces, and sulci orient the external heart.
recognitionCues: Apex points inferiorly and leftward; base is the broad superior/posterior aspect.
The coronary sulcus is the atrioventricular groove visible around the heart.
landmarks: Coronary sulcus separates atria from ventricles; the apex is formed mainly by the left ventricle.
relationships: The base receives and gives rise to the great vessels, while the apex is the inferior tip.
commonConfusions: Base is not the inferior tip; the coronary sulcus is not the interventricular sulcus.

lessons.title: Chambers and septa
lessons.summary: Atria receive blood, ventricles eject blood, and septa separate circuits.
recognitionCues: Auricles are ear-like appendages of the atria; right and left chambers are not interchangeable.
The right auricle projects from the right atrium and the left auricle from the left atrium.
landmarks: The interatrial septum separates the atria; the interventricular septum lies between ventricles.
relationships: Chambers connect through valves and great vessels; the pericardial cavity surrounds the heart.
commonConfusions: An auricle is not an atrium as a whole; a septum is not a valve; the interatrial septum is not interventricular.

lessons.title: Valves and wall
lessons.summary: Valves enforce one-way flow while wall layers provide contraction and lining.
recognitionCues: Chordae attach AV valve cusps to papillary muscles; epicardium is visceral serous pericardium.
Fibrous pericardium is the tough outer sac; serous pericardium is the smooth double-layered lining.

From above with posterior at the top, the tricuspid orifice is on the anatomical right of the mitral orifice. The smaller aortic and pulmonary valves have three semilunar cusps; aortic lies behind pulmonary in this drawing.
landmarks: Myocardium is the thick contractile middle layer; fibrous pericardium is external to serous pericardium.
The pericardial cavity is between parietal and visceral serous layers, not inside the myocardium.
relationships: Serous pericardium has parietal and visceral layers around the pericardial cavity; epicardium is the visceral layer on the heart.

The tricuspid and mitral valves lie between atria and ventricles. Their leaflets are tethered by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles; the semilunar valves guard the arterial outlets without chordae.
commonConfusions: Mitral is left AV; tricuspid is right AV; epicardium is not myocardium; pericardial cavity is not a wall layer.
Left and right in a superior view are anatomical positions, not a promise about the viewer’s screen side. A labeled plate is for Study, not an unlabeled identification question.

lessons.title: Coronary circulation
lessons.summary: Coronary arteries occupy sulci and cardiac veins converge on the coronary sinus.
recognitionCues: Coronary vessels lie on the heart surface; the great cardiac vein accompanies the anterior interventricular artery.
The right and left coronary arteries arise near the aortic root; the left coronary divides into anterior interventricular and circumflex branches.
landmarks: Anterior and posterior interventricular arteries occupy their respective sulci; right marginal follows the acute margin.
The circumflex artery follows the coronary sulcus; middle cardiac vein accompanies the posterior interventricular artery.
relationships: Cardiac veins converge on the coronary sinus, which drains to the right atrium; great, middle, and small cardiac veins occupy corresponding surface routes.
commonConfusions: Coronary arteries are not pulmonary arteries; a cardiac vein is not a vena cava; anterior and posterior interventricular vessels are not interchangeable.

lessons.title: Conduction system
lessons.summary: The cardiac impulse travels from pacemaker to ventricular conducting fibers.
recognitionCues: SA node precedes AV node.
landmarks: AV bundle enters the interventricular septum.
relationships: Conduction coordinates atrial then ventricular contraction.
commonConfusions: Purkinje fibers do not initiate the normal rhythm.

lessons.title: Great vessels and flow
lessons.summary: Great vessels connect pulmonary and systemic circuits to the four chambers.
recognitionCues: Pulmonary arteries leave the right ventricle; pulmonary veins enter the left atrium.
The SVC and IVC enter the right atrium; the ascending aorta begins at the left ventricle.
landmarks: The aortic arch gives rise to the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, and left subclavian arteries; the pulmonary trunk divides into right and left pulmonary arteries.
relationships: Vessel identity follows its chamber connection and oxygenation route; ascending, arch, and descending aorta are continuous segments.
commonConfusions: Pulmonary arteries are arteries despite carrying deoxygenated blood; the left arch branches are not pulmonary branches; pulmonary veins are not venae cavae.

lessons.title: Blood as a connective tissue
lessons.summary: Separate the liquid matrix from circulating cells and cell fragments before studying a smear.
recognitionCues: Blood has a liquid extracellular matrix (plasma) and formed elements: erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets.
Centrifuged anticoagulated blood separates into plasma above, a thin leukocyte/platelet buffy coat, and packed erythrocytes below.
landmarks: Serum is the liquid left after blood has clotted; unlike plasma, it lacks the clotting factors consumed or removed during clotting.
relationships: The buffy coat concentrates white cells and platelets, not just erythrocytes. A peripheral smear spreads the formed elements on a slide rather than showing a plasma layer.
commonConfusions: Platelets are fragments, not full leukocytes.
Plasma is not the same specimen as serum, and a smear is not a centrifuged blood tube.

lessons.title: Red cells and platelets
lessons.summary: Use relative size, a nucleus, and central pallor to separate the common formed elements in a stained smear.
recognitionCues: Mature erythrocytes are numerous, anucleate biconcave discs; their thin centers often appear paler than their edges.
Platelets are tiny anucleate cytoplasmic fragments, much smaller than erythrocytes, and may appear as purple specks or small clusters.
landmarks: Megakaryocytes are large cells in red bone marrow that shed platelets; they are not normal circulating smear cells.
relationships: Biconcavity increases erythrocyte surface area for gas exchange; platelets provide a first structural plug at a damaged vessel.
commonConfusions: A pale erythrocyte center is not a nucleus.
A platelet is not a miniature erythrocyte or a whole megakaryocyte.

lessons.title: Five leukocytes at a glance
lessons.summary: Identify the five main leukocytes by nuclear shape and staining, with approximate normal abundance as context.
recognitionCues: Granulocytes: neutrophils have fine pale granules and a segmented nucleus (usually 2–5 lobes); eosinophils have coarse red-orange granules and usually a two-lobed nucleus; basophils have dark blue-purple granules often obscuring the nucleus.
Agranulocytes: a small lymphocyte has a large round nucleus and thin cytoplasmic rim; a monocyte is larger with an indented or kidney-shaped nucleus and more cytoplasm.
landmarks: In a typical adult differential, neutrophils are most frequent (about 50–70%), lymphocytes next (about 20–30%); monocytes (about 2–8%) and eosinophils (about 2–4%) are less frequent, and basophils are rarest (under 1%). Ranges overlap and vary.
relationships: “Agranular” means no prominent stain-visible granules, not no granules at all; all five types are leukocytes, unlike anucleate red cells and platelet fragments.
commonConfusions: Eosinophil granules stain red-orange, not the deep purple of basophils.
A segmented neutrophil is not a round-nucleated lymphocyte.

lessons.title: Where formed elements originate
lessons.summary: Connect adult red bone marrow to blood-cell lineages without memorizing detailed maturation stages.
recognitionCues: Hematopoiesis takes place mainly in red bone marrow after birth; marrow stem cells ultimately yield red cells, white cells, and platelet-producing megakaryocytes.
Adult red marrow is concentrated in axial bones and proximal ends of the humerus and femur.
landmarks: A marrow sample can show large nucleated megakaryocytes; a peripheral blood smear shows their much smaller released platelet fragments.
relationships: Blood is a connective tissue continually renewed from marrow; erythrocytes lose their nuclei as they mature, while leukocytes retain nuclei.
commonConfusions: Yellow marrow is not the main routine blood-producing tissue.
Circulating platelets are made by megakaryocytes, not by erythrocytes.

lessons.title: Read a peripheral blood smear
lessons.summary: Apply a fixed visual checklist to a stained smear without assuming the description is an actual image.
recognitionCues: First distinguish many pale-centered anucleate red discs from tiny platelet fragments and the fewer nucleated white cells.
For a white cell, compare nuclear form (segmented, round, indented, or bilobed), cytoplasm, and granule color before naming it.
landmarks: Segmented pale-granule cell → neutrophil; round nucleus with thin rim → small lymphocyte; larger indented nucleus → monocyte; orange-red coarse granules → eosinophil; dense dark purple granules → basophil.
relationships: Smear identification is based on morphology; abundance helps prioritize a likely answer but does not replace nucleus and granule cues.
commonConfusions: Descriptions here are text-only recognition practice, not labeled micrographs.
Do not identify every purple speck as a basophil: platelets are tiny and lack a nucleus.

lessons.title: Vessel wall
lessons.summary: Tunics vary with pressure and vessel function.
recognitionCues: Endothelium forms the inner lining.
landmarks: Media is smooth-muscle-rich.
relationships: Wall composition predicts compliance and resistance.
An atherosclerotic plaque builds within an arterial wall and narrows the normally open lumen; it is not a normal capillary wall layer.
commonConfusions: Tunica externa is not the lumen.

lessons.title: Vessel types
lessons.summary: Arteries, capillaries, and veins form a continuous route.
recognitionCues: Capillaries have the simplest wall.
landmarks: Arterioles lead into capillary beds.
relationships: Pressure falls from arteries toward veins.
commonConfusions: Venules are not arteries.

lessons.title: Capillary types
lessons.summary: Continuous, fenestrated, and sinusoid capillaries differ in permeability.
recognitionCues: Sinusoids have the largest gaps.
landmarks: Fenestrations permit greater exchange.
relationships: Permeability matches local tissue needs.
commonConfusions: A capillary type is not a tunic.

lessons.title: Blood elements
lessons.summary: Formed elements have distinct cellular or fragment morphology.
recognitionCues: Platelets are cell fragments.
landmarks: Erythrocytes are abundant formed elements.
relationships: Cell form supports transport or defense.
commonConfusions: Platelets are not leukocytes.

lessons.title: Regional vessels
lessons.summary: Named arterial and venous routes identify regions and clinical access points.
recognitionCues: Brachial lies in the arm; femoral lies in the thigh; popliteal lies behind the knee.
The common carotid ascends the neck before dividing into internal and external carotid arteries.
landmarks: The axillary artery continues as brachial; radial and ulnar arteries supply the forearm. Cephalic and median cubital veins are superficial.
Femoral continues to popliteal behind the knee, then to anterior and posterior tibial routes in the leg; internal jugular drains the deep neck.
relationships: Carotid, upper-limb, and lower-limb names mark continuous regional routes; the subclavian-to-axillary-to-brachial sequence crosses the upper limb.
commonConfusions: Internal and external carotid are not the common carotid; brachial is not brachiocephalic; anterior tibial is not posterior tibial; an artery is not defined by oxygen content.

lessons.title: Central arterial branches and great veins
lessons.summary: The aorta and major great veins give named routes to and from body regions.
recognitionCues: The celiac trunk and renal arteries arise from the abdominal aorta.
The celiac trunk serves upper abdominal branches; renal arteries run laterally to the kidneys.
landmarks: Brachiocephalic veins unite to form the superior vena cava; subclavian veins continue from the upper limbs toward that confluence.
relationships: Named branches preserve the route from aorta to organs and from upper limbs to the SVC.
commonConfusions: Brachiocephalic trunk is arterial; brachiocephalic veins are venous; the celiac trunk is not the hepatic portal vein.

lessons.title: Portal circulation
lessons.summary: Portal blood passes from digestive organs through liver sinusoids before systemic return.
recognitionCues: Portal vein enters the liver; hepatic veins leave it.
landmarks: Sinusoids lie between portal inflow and hepatic-vein outflow.
relationships: Two capillary beds are connected in series.
commonConfusions: Hepatic portal and hepatic veins have opposite route roles.

lessons.title: Flow sequence
lessons.summary: Regional vessels can be traced from aorta through exchange beds to veins.
recognitionCues: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
landmarks: Veins return blood toward the heart.
relationships: Microcirculation links both sides.
commonConfusions: Direction, not oxygen content, defines artery.

lessons.title: Large artery structure
lessons.summary: Elastic and muscular arteries distribute or regulate blood flow.
recognitionCues: Aorta is elastic; muscular arteries distribute blood to regional territories.
landmarks: Elastic recoil supports continuous flow; muscular arteries have a prominent smooth-muscle media for regional distribution.
relationships: The aorta is an elastic artery; muscular arteries regulate regional distribution without using common carotid as a generic example.
commonConfusions: Elastic does not mean skeletal muscle; common carotid anatomy is covered in the regional-vessels lesson.

lessons.title: Venous return
lessons.summary: Veins and venules collect low-pressure blood from tissues.
recognitionCues: Venules receive capillary blood.
landmarks: Superficial veins have recognizable regional names.
relationships: Veins complete the return route.
commonConfusions: A venule is smaller than a vein.

lessons.title: Upper airway
lessons.summary: The nasal passages condition inhaled air before it reaches the larynx.
recognitionCues: Orient by position, continuity, and distinctive wall or tissue features.
Compare adjacent structures before selecting a label.
Nasal conchae project from the lateral nasal wall; the choanae open posteriorly into the nasopharynx.
landmarks: Use named boundaries, layers, and connected passages as landmarks.
relationships: Location predicts the structure’s contribution to the organ pathway or function.
The nasal conchae, hard palate, and choanae mark the transition from the nasal cavity to the pharynx.
commonConfusions: Do not substitute a neighboring structure or a different tissue layer.
Do not confuse a nasal concha with a paranasal sinus or the nasal septum.

lessons.title: Larynx and conducting tree
lessons.summary: The glottis comprises the true vocal folds and rima glottidis; the rima glottidis is the opening.
recognitionCues: Orient by position, continuity, and distinctive wall or tissue features.
Compare adjacent structures before selecting a label.
The laryngeal inlet leads to the vestibule; the glottis comprises the true vocal folds and the rima glottidis, whose rima is the opening.
landmarks: Use named boundaries, layers, and connected passages as landmarks.
relationships: Location predicts the structure’s contribution to the organ pathway or function.
The cricoid is the complete laryngeal ring and the trachealis bridges the posterior tracheal cartilage.
commonConfusions: Do not substitute a neighboring structure or a different tissue layer.
The laryngeal inlet and rima glottidis are openings; the glottis is the vocal-fold/rima unit, not a cartilage.

lessons.title: Lungs and pleura
lessons.summary: Lobes, fissures, hilum, and pleura orient the lungs in the thorax.
recognitionCues: Orient by position, continuity, and distinctive wall or tissue features.
Compare adjacent structures before selecting a label.
The right lung has superior, middle, and inferior lobes; the left has superior and inferior lobes plus a cardiac notch. The hilum is the surface gateway, while the root is the bundle entering it.
landmarks: Use named boundaries, layers, and connected passages as landmarks.
relationships: Location predicts the structure’s contribution to the organ pathway or function.
Visceral pleura adheres to the lung, parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall and diaphragm, and the pleural cavity lies between them.
commonConfusions: Do not substitute a neighboring structure or a different tissue layer.
Do not call the hilum the root: the hilum is an area, whereas the root contains the bronchus, vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.

lessons.title: Respiratory zone
lessons.summary: Alveoli and their thin capillary interface enable gas exchange.
recognitionCues: Orient by position, continuity, and distinctive wall or tissue features.
Compare adjacent structures before selecting a label.
Alveolar septa contain pulmonary capillaries and form the thin interface between adjacent air spaces.
landmarks: Use named boundaries, layers, and connected passages as landmarks.
relationships: Location predicts the structure’s contribution to the organ pathway or function.
The alveolar septum combines epithelium, shared basement membrane, and capillary endothelium in the respiratory membrane.
In emphysema, walls between alveoli are damaged, leaving fewer intact septa than in normal small air spaces.
commonConfusions: Do not substitute a neighboring structure or a different tissue layer.
An alveolar duct is a passage with alveolar openings; an alveolar septum is a wall between air spaces.

lessons.title: Respiratory histology
lessons.summary: Epithelium, secretory cells, elastic tissue, and pneumocytes distinguish airway slides.
recognitionCues: Orient by position, continuity, and distinctive wall or tissue features.
Compare adjacent structures before selecting a label.
Tracheal ciliated pseudostratified epithelium contains goblet cells; bronchioles have smaller airways with smooth muscle, while alveoli show thin type I cells and cuboidal type II cells.
landmarks: Use named boundaries, layers, and connected passages as landmarks.
relationships: Location predicts the structure’s contribution to the organ pathway or function.
Elastic fibers support recoil in the respiratory tree; type II pneumocytes occupy alveolar surfaces and secrete surfactant, while macrophages lie in air spaces.
commonConfusions: Do not substitute a neighboring structure or a different tissue layer.
A terminal bronchiole is conducting and lacks alveoli in its wall; a respiratory bronchiole has alveolar outpouchings.

lessons.title: Ventilation relationships
lessons.summary: Diaphragm movement and pleural coupling change lung volume.
recognitionCues: Orient by position, continuity, and distinctive wall or tissue features.
Compare adjacent structures before selecting a label.
Parietal pleura lines the inner thoracic wall and diaphragm; visceral pleura follows the lung surface, with the pleural cavity between them.
landmarks: Use named boundaries, layers, and connected passages as landmarks.
relationships: Location predicts the structure’s contribution to the organ pathway or function.
The diaphragm forms the inferior thoracic boundary, and pleural coupling links thoracic-wall movement to the lung surface.
commonConfusions: Do not substitute a neighboring structure or a different tissue layer.
Pleural cavity is a potential space, not a third pleural layer; visceral and parietal pleura are the two layers.

lessons.title: Airflow sequence
lessons.summary: Trace air from the nasal cavity to an alveolus through the conducting and respiratory zones.
recognitionCues: Orient by position, continuity, and distinctive wall or tissue features.
Compare adjacent structures before selecting a label.

The route is nasal cavity, nasopharynx, oropharynx, laryngopharynx, larynx, and trachea; the trachea ends at the carina and divides into main bronchi, then lobar, segmental, and smaller bronchi/bronchioles, terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchiole, alveolar duct, then alveolus.
landmarks: Use named boundaries, layers, and connected passages as landmarks.
relationships: Location predicts the structure’s contribution to the organ pathway or function.
The carina is the tracheal bifurcation landmark, not a conduit; the terminal bronchiole ends the conducting zone, while respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts begin the respiratory zone.
commonConfusions: Do not substitute a neighboring structure or a different tissue layer.
Do not treat the carina as a tube or skip the pharyngeal subdivisions; terminal bronchiole precedes respiratory bronchiole.
